questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: predict the ion event at threshold
questions.stem: A neuron is resting near minus 70 millivolts. Once a stimulus pushes the membrane to threshold, what ion event is responsible for the rapid rise of the action potential?

options.text: Sodium ions rush into the axon through open channels
Potassium ions rush into the axon through open channels
options.misconception: thinks potassium floods inward, reversing the direction of its flow during a spike

options.text: Chloride ions leave the axon to balance the charge
options.misconception: believes chloride efflux, not sodium influx, drives the rising phase

options.text: The sodium-potassium pump pushes three sodium ions inward
options.misconception: assumes the pump directly creates the spike and can work fast enough to do so

questions.explanation: At threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium follows its concentration gradient into the negatively charged interior, which makes the membrane swing positive. Potassium leaves later to repolarize, chloride buffers rather than drives the rise, and the sodium-potassium pump works too slowly to account for a millisecond-timescale spike.
questions.hint: Which ion is far more concentrated outside the cell than inside?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: interpret the phases of a voltage trace
questions.stem: A voltage-versus-time trace rises from minus 70 to about plus 30 millivolts, falls past minus 70 to about minus 80, then flattens. Which phase is produced by potassium channels staying open after the sodium channels have closed?

options.text: The steep rise from minus 70 to plus 30
options.misconception: misreads the rising phase as a potassium effect rather than an influx of sodium

options.text: The dip below minus 80 millivolts after the fall
The flat baseline before the spike fires
options.misconception: confuses the resting plateau with a later phase of the trace

options.text: The moment the membrane crosses minus 55 millivolts
options.misconception: identifies the threshold crossing as the cause of the undershoot

questions.explanation: The undershoot, called hyperpolarization, happens because potassium channels close slowly, so potassium keeps leaving the cell after enough has already exited to restore minus 70 millivolts. The steep rise belongs to sodium influx, the flat line is the resting state, and crossing threshold only initiates the sequence.
questions.hint: Look for the portion of the trace that falls below the resting value.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why a neuron either fires a full-sized action potential or does not fire at all, regardless of whether the stimulus barely reaches threshold or far exceeds it.

answer.exemplar: Once threshold is reached, voltage-gated sodium channels open and let sodium enter, which depolarizes the membrane further and opens still more sodium channels in a positive-feedback loop. That loop runs to completion, so every spike reaches the same peak of about plus 30 millivolts. Because the channels are either enough to trigger the loop or not enough to start it, a stronger stimulus cannot produce a bigger spike; instead it raises the number of spikes fired per second.

questions.explanation: The all-or-none law follows from positive-feedback opening of sodium channels: past threshold the avalanche completes itself, so intensity is coded by firing rate rather than spike size. Sub-threshold stimuli die out as graded potentials because the feedback loop never gets started.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the sodium channels once depolarization starts to feed back on itself.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A medication binds receptors for a neurotransmitter without activating them, so the natural messenger is blocked. Explain the difference between this compound's effect and that of a molecule which mimics the messenger.

answer.exemplar: The blocking compound is an antagonist: it occupies the receptor but produces no response, so the postsynaptic cell receives less signaling than usual. A molecule that mimics the messenger is an agonist: it occupies the receptor and activates it, so the cell responds as if the natural transmitter were present. For example, an antagonist at acetylcholine receptors on muscle fibers weakens contraction, while an agonist at the same sites can trigger cramping or sustained contraction.

questions.explanation: The distinction is activation versus occupancy: antagonists occupy receptors without firing them, so signaling drops, while agonists occupy and fire them, so signaling rises. Both compete with the natural messenger, but only one produces a downstream response.
questions.hint: Ask what happens inside the postsynaptic cell while the compound is bound.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain how a released neurotransmitter is deactivated and why that step is essential for clear signaling.

answer.exemplar: Clearance happens by several converging routes: transmitter is removed by reuptake transporters into the presynaptic terminal or into glia, broken down by enzymes in the synaptic cleft, or diffuses away from the receptors. Without that clearance, the molecules would keep binding receptors and the postsynaptic cell would stay stimulated, so it could not register the arrival of a new message. Phasic bursts would blur into a constant tone, and the timing that carries information would be lost.

questions.explanation: Deactivation removes transmitter from receptors so the synapse can reset between messages. If clearance fails, receptor occupancy becomes continuous and the difference between one signal and the next disappears, which is why reuptake and enzyme breakdown matter as much as release does.
questions.hint: Think about what the postsynaptic cell experiences if nothing clears the messenger.

questions.hint: Compare the first dose with the same dose taken later.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain how myelination produces saltatory conduction and why regeneration at the gaps is still necessary.

answer.exemplar: Myelin wraps the axon in fatty layers that keep ions from crossing the membrane, so the current generated at one active spot travels along the inside of the axon instead of leaking out. The voltage decays with distance, though, so if no new channels were available the signal would fade before reaching the end. The bare gaps between myelin segments are packed with sodium and potassium channels, and at each gap the arriving current reopens sodium channels and regenerates a full-sized spike. The signal therefore appears to leap from gap to gap, which is far faster than continuous crawling and uses less energy.

questions.explanation: Insulation preserves the current and the nodes regenerate it, so the signal leaps rather than fades. Without nodes the electrical signal would attenuate over distance, which is why both the myelin wrap and the gaps are needed for efficient conduction.
questions.hint: Consider what the current does between gaps and what happens when it reaches one.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain how several weak inputs arriving at different dendrites can together trigger an action potential, and why their position on the dendrite tree matters.

answer.exemplar: Each weak input produces only a small depolarization that spreads passively and decays with distance from its source. When several arrive close together in time, or at nearby locations, their voltages add: if the summed depolarization at the trigger zone still crosses threshold, an action potential fires. The trigger zone, at the axon hillock, is packed with the highest density of voltage-gated sodium channels, so it is where summation is most likely to reach threshold. Inputs landing far out on distal dendrites decay before they can contribute, which is why location along the tree changes the weight an input carries.

questions.explanation: Summation of graded potentials reaches threshold most easily where channel density is highest, at the axon hillock. Distal inputs decay passively, so distance reduces their influence, and no single weak input can trigger a spike on its own.
questions.hint: Consider how graded potentials spread and where the channels are concentrated.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why damage to the hippocampus leaves old memories intact but prevents the formation of new ones.

answer.exemplar: The hippocampus binds a new experience into a lasting memory trace but is not itself the permanent store for memories laid down long ago. Once a memory has been consolidated, its trace is distributed across cortical networks, so a hippocampal lesion erases the ability to lay down new traces rather than everything already stored. That is why a person with such damage can still recall childhood events yet re-asks the same question the next day: the older consolidated traces survive, and only new consolidation fails.

questions.explanation: Consolidation is a transfer process: the hippocampus encodes experiences, then cortical networks hold the durable trace. Old traces no longer depend on the hippocampus, while new ones still need it, which produces the classic pattern of intact recall with failed new learning.
questions.hint: Distinguish the structure that writes memories from the places that keep them.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why the same neurotransmitter can be excitatory at one synapse and inhibitory at another, and state what determines that difference.

answer.exemplar: The effect depends entirely on the receptor and the channel it opens, not on the messenger itself. If the receptor opens a channel that lets positive charge in, the postsynaptic cell moves toward firing and the result is excitatory. If the receptor opens a chloride channel or closes a cation channel, the cell is held away from firing and the result is inhibitory. So the same molecule that depolarizes one target can hyperpolarize another, and the determining factor is the receptor subtype together with the ion that flows through it.

questions.explanation: Receptor subtype and ion selectivity set the sign of the response. That is why one chemical messenger can excite one target and inhibit another, and why drug design targets specific receptors rather than the transmitter itself.
questions.hint: Start from what the receptor opens, not from what the molecule is.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why a neuron encodes the intensity of a stimulus by firing rate instead of by spike height.

answer.exemplar: Every spike reaches the same peak because threshold sets off a self-completing inflow of sodium, so amplitude cannot encode anything. What can vary is how fast the spikes come. A strong stimulus keeps the membrane above threshold, so it crosses threshold again and again and produces a high firing frequency, while a weak one just barely crosses and fires rarely. The nervous system therefore reads intensity from the count of spikes per second, which is why a bright light yields a faster train of signals than a dim one.

questions.explanation: Amplitude is fixed by the all-or-none property, so only the frequency of spikes is free to carry information about strength. The neuron counts events over time, and later stages of the brain decode that rate.
questions.hint: Ask what still varies once every spike is the same size.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain the function of the refractory period
questions.stem: Explain why the refractory period is necessary for reliable one-way conduction along an axon.

answer.exemplar: Once a stretch of membrane fires, its sodium channels are inactivated and cannot fire again until they recover, so the stretch just traveled is temporarily unresponsive while the stretch ahead is still ready. The impulse therefore can only move forward into fresh membrane, because the region behind cannot be re-excited. If there were no refractory period, the local currents could re-excite the region behind the spike and the signal could reverberate or travel in both directions, scrambling the message.

questions.explanation: Sodium channel inactivation behind the spike makes re-excitation impossible in the region already passed, so the signal advances only into ready membrane. The refractory period therefore both enforces direction and sets a ceiling on firing rate.
questions.hint: Ask what the membrane behind the spike is doing while the region ahead is still excitable.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain how researchers can observe reorganization of a cortical map after a region is damaged.

answer.exemplar: Researchers stimulate or image the cortex repeatedly and measure which sites produce which effects. After damage removes part of a map, the neighboring regions that remain often begin to respond in ways they did not before, so a site that once controlled one part of the body may come to control another. The change appears gradually over weeks, and it correlates with recovery of the lost function. Repeating the mapping at several time points makes the shift visible, because the borders of the map move on the cortical surface.

questions.explanation: Repeated mapping reveals that the borders of a cortical representation shift after damage, which is why the map is described as plastic rather than fixed. The signature is a neighboring site taking over the lost function over time.
questions.hint: Think about what a mapping study would show if the same site produced a different effect later.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a claim about transmitter release
questions.stem: A classmate claims that a stronger input makes a single presynaptic neuron release more transmitter per spike, which is why the response feels stronger. What is the best evaluation?

options.text: The claim is exactly right for every synapse
options.misconception: accepts the claim without noting the all-or-none nature of a spike

options.text: Release per spike is stereotyped; strength shows in rate
Stronger inputs block release instead of raising it
options.misconception: reverses the relationship rather than correcting its mechanism

options.text: Release per spike varies with mood and attention
options.misconception: attributes spike properties to distant modulatory states

questions.explanation: Because a single spike is all-or-none, the amount of transmitter released per spike at a given terminal is broadly stereotyped rather than graded by stimulus strength. A stronger input is coded as a higher frequency of spikes, and postsynaptic summation of those spikes produces the larger response. Modulation and attention do change synaptic efficacy, but not by scaling release within one spike.
